claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among the equiatomic quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys are not explained simply by constituent count.
Differences in local chemical short-range order alter the stacking-fault-energy landscape across these alloys.
Specific elemental interactions in equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni produce a lower effective stacking-fault energy than in its quaternary and ternary subsets.
Lower effective stacking-fault energy in the quinary alloy promotes more planar dislocation slip.
Lower effective stacking-fault energy in the quinary alloy increases its propensity for deformation twinning.
Greater planar slip and deformation twinning enhance strain hardening in the quinary alloy.
Greater planar slip and deformation twinning delay necking in the quinary alloy relative to the quaternary and ternary alloys.
The compared alloys can be prepared by identical thermomechanical routes as single-phase FCC materials with similar grain sizes.
Local chemical short-range order modulates effective stacking-fault energy.
Effective stacking-fault energy controls the balance of dislocation slip and deformation twinning.
Chemical-ordering effects are less pronounced in the quaternary and ternary alloys than in the quinary alloy.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will have higher effective stacking-fault energies.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will exhibit less planar slip and deformation twinning.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will exhibit lower strain-hardening rates.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will undergo necking earlier.
The proposed comparison is applicable to single-phase FCC alloys subjected to identical thermomechanical processing and tensile deformation at room temperature and quasi-static strain rates.
Solid-solution-strengthening differences may also contribute to the observed mechanical-property differences.
